content: Whole-body massage for newborns, with or without the use of oil, has been studied in comparison to no massage. The evidence regarding its effects on various newborn and infant outcomes is of very low certainty, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. Below are the findings: 1. Growth Outcomes: It is unclear whether whole-body massage has any impact on newborn weight at the end of the intervention period or at follow-up between 8 to 12 months. Similarly, its effect on infant length at 12 months is uncertain. 2. Head Circumference: There is no clear evidence to suggest that whole-body massage affects head circumference at the end of the intervention period or at six months of follow-up. 3. Severe Neonatal/Infant Morbidity: The effect of whole-body massage on bilirubin levels in newborns four days after birth is uncertain. 4. Sleep Characteristics: It is unclear whether massage influences newborn sleep duration at the end of the intervention period or at 24 months of follow-up. 5. Neurodevelopment: The impact of whole-body massage on psychomotor and mental development index scores, as well as gross motor, fine motor, language, and social behavior development, remains uncertain at the end of the intervention period or at follow-up. 6. Adverse Effects: No adverse effects were reported in the included studies. Maternal Outcomes: Maternal Functioning and Well-being: The effect of newborn massage on maternal attachment inventory scores is uncertain. Similarly, its impact on crying or fussing time at the end of the intervention period and at six months of follow-up is unclear. Additional Considerations: A 2013 Cochrane Review of 34 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) suggested potential benefits of massage in terms of weight, length, head circumference growth, and developmental outcomes. However, the quality of evidence was rated very low. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis on massage for hyperbilirubinemia found that massage therapy significantly reduced transcutaneous bilirubin levels after four days in full-term neonates. However, these findings may not apply to healthy newborns, as the population studied included jaundiced infants. Values and Preferences: Women value postnatal care that helps them adapt to their new identity as mothers, develop confidence, and adjust to changes in relationships and daily life. They prioritize therapies that enhance infant development, promote sleep, and reduce crying. Feasibility and Acceptability: Infant massage is a simple, low-cost intervention that can be performed by parents or caregivers with proper training. Women generally appreciate practical and accessible therapies that improve their baby’s comfort and well-being. Fathers who participated in infant massage reported benefits such as reduced infant stress, increased confidence, and a stronger bond with their child. Recommendations: 1. Responsive Care: All infants and children should receive responsive care from birth to three years of age. Parents and caregivers should be supported to provide such care, which includes recognizing and responding to the child’s signals appropriately. 2. Early Learning Activities: Parents and caregivers should engage in early learning activities with their infants and children, such as making eye contact, smiling, talking, singing, and gentle massage. 3. Maternal Mental Health: Psychosocial interventions to support maternal mental health should be integrated into early childhood health and development services. 4. Exclusive Breastfeeding: All babies should be exclusively breastfed from birth until six months of age, with mothers receiving counseling and support at each postnatal contact. Health System Considerations: High-quality postnatal care should include structured schedules for postnatal contacts, tailored to the needs of the mother and newborn. A minimum of four postnatal care contacts is recommended, with the first occurring within 24 hours of birth. Involving men in postnatal care can improve maternal and newborn health outcomes by providing practical, emotional, and financial support. Conclusion: While whole-body massage for newborns shows potential benefits, the evidence is of very low certainty, and further high-quality research is needed to confirm its effects on growth, development, and other outcomes.
